{{Short description|Concept in topology}}
In mathematics, especially in [[algebraic topology]], the '''mapping space''' between two spaces is the space of all the (continuous) maps between them.

Viewing the set of all the maps as a space is useful because that allows for topological considerations. For example, a [[curve]] <math>h: I \to \operatorname{Map}(X, Y)</math> in the mapping space is exactly a [[homotopy]] between the starting point and the end point.

From the [[category theory]] point of view, a mapping space provides the [[internal Hom]] (i.e., hom that is also an object) in the category of spaces.

== Topologies ==
{{expand section|date=November 2024}}

A mapping space can be equipped with several topologies. A common one is the [[compact-open topology]] or the [[k-ification]] of it. Typically, there is then the adjoint relation
:<math>\operatorname{Map}(X \times Y, Z) \simeq \operatorname{Map}(X, \operatorname{Map}(Y, Z))</math>
and thus <math>\operatorname{Map}</math> is an analog of the [[Hom functor]]. (For pathological spaces, this relation may fail.)

Here is another common one. We have:
:<math>\operatorname{Map}(X, Y) \hookrightarrow X \times Y</math>
given by <math>f \mapsto \Gamma_f = </math> the graph of <math>f</math>. Then we can give <math>\operatorname{Map}(X, Y)</math> the [[Whitney topology]] (also called the [[fine topology (differential topology)|fine topology]] or the [[strong topology]]) where a basic open set consists of those <math>g</math> such that <math>\Gamma_g \subset U</math> for some open subset <math>U \subset X \times Y</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hirsch|1997|loc=Ch. 2., § 4.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Wall|2016|loc=§ A.4.}}</ref> The compact-open topology does not handle a behavior at infinity well and so sometimes the Whitney topology is used instead.

If <math>X</math> is a paracompact<ref>Editorial note: why is "paracompact" needed?</ref> and <math>Y</math> is a metric space, then the Whitney topology has a basic open set of the form
:<math>B(f, \epsilon) := \{ g \mid d(g(x), f(x)) < \epsilon(x) \}</math>
for some <math>f \in \operatorname{Map}(X, Y)</math> and some continuous function <math>\epsilon : X \to \mathbb{R}_{> 0}</math>. 
If, moreover, <math>Y</math> is complete, then we have the following important fact:
:Let <math>Q \subset \operatorname{Map}(X, Y)</math> be a subset such that every uniform limit of a sequence in <math>Q</math>, if any, is in <math>Q</math>. Then <math>Q</math> is a [[Baire space]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hirsch|1997|loc=Ch. 2., § 4., Theorem 4.2.}}</ref>
This is proved by the same way [[Baire's category theorem]] is proved except we use the above family-version of a ball.

== Smooth mappings ==
{{expand section|date=April 2026}}
{{main|Whitney topologies}}
For manifolds <math>M, N</math>, there is the subset <math>\mathcal{C}^r(M, N) \subset \operatorname{Map}(M, N)</math> that consists of all the <math> \mathcal{C}^r</math>-smooth maps from <math>M</math> to <math>N</math>. It can be equipped with the weak or strong topology.

A basic approximation theorem says that <math>\mathcal{C}_W^s(M, N)</math> is dense in <math>\mathcal{C}_S^r(M, N)</math> for <math>1 \le s \le \infty, 0 \le r < s</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hirsch|1997|loc=Ch. 2., § 2., Theorem 2.6.}}</ref>

See also: [[Grauert's approximation theorem]]

== Homotopy type of a mapping space ==
A basic result here is a theorem of Milnor which says that the mapping space <math>\operatorname{Map}(X, Y)</math> has the homotopy type of a CW-complex if <math>X</math> is a compact Hausdorff space and <math>Y</math> has the homotopy type of a CW-complex.<ref>{{harvnb|Milnor|1959|loc=Theorem 3.}}</ref>
